answer.rationale: A HARA (hazard analysis and risk assessment, ISO 26262-3) is performed at the vehicle/item level on the item definition only. It identifies hazards, rates them (S/E/C) and derives ASILs and safety goals. It depends on the item's functions, boundaries and operational situations, which come from the item definition. It does not depend on implementation artifacts such as core allocation, task timing, memory parameters, code, MPU partitions, interconnect, DMA, CAN matrix, built images or test rig, because those are design decisions made downstream of the HARA. It also consumes no other evidence item. Rather, the safety goals it produces are inputs to the downstream analyses (RTA, INT, MPU, E2E, etc.). TARA is a parallel cybersecurity analysis, not an input to the HARA.

answer.rationale: HIL is an empirical end-to-end latency measurement, so it depends on the rig configuration and on the actual built software that was executed. That covers the island image containing BrakeCtl and the other island tasks, and the application image that generated the concurrent production load. Because the report says the result includes shared-SRAM contention, it also depends on: the interconnect configuration (port arbitration, slot latency, which clusters reach the port); the application-cluster DMA engine, which also contends at the port; and all core allocation rows, which determine what runs on I0/I1 and A0-A3 during the test. Task source code, MPU partition entries and E2E library code affect the result only through the built images, so they are covered by img.island and img.app and are not listed separately; a reviewer may choose to list them explicitly. Analytical timing and memory parameters (tim.*, mem.*) are model inputs and do not change measured behaviour. CAN/E2E artifacts are excluded because the report does not say the measured path crosses CAN; a reviewer should add can and code.e2e if it does. The test is a direct measurement and does not consume the results of other evidence items such as INT, RTA, SA or UT.

answer.rationale: HARA (hazard analysis and risk assessment) is done at the vehicle/item level. Its result is the hazards, ASILs and safety goals. These come only from the item definition (rev 4): its functions, operating situations and boundaries. It is performed before, and independent of, the implementation, so no implementation artifact belongs in scope. This excludes core allocation, task timing, memory and code, MPU partitions, the interconnect, DMA, CAN, images and the rig. It consumes no other evidence. The dependency runs the other way: later analyses (RTA, INT, MPU, E2E, HIL, etc.) and the safety goals derived from them consume HARA. TARA is a parallel security analysis of the same item definition, not an input to HARA, so it is not included.

answer.rationale: INT is an on-target measurement of shared-SRAM port contention. The report states it relies on the task-to-core mapping, so all six allocation rows are in scope. It also relies on the interconnect arbitration, so ic is in scope; ic also defines slot latency and which clusters are wired to the port. The result depends on the normal load of every core that reaches the port. That load is set by each task's memory-access parameters (mem.*), its actual access behaviour (code.* and the built images img.island and img.app that ran on target), and its activation rate and execution time (tim.*, since a period or WCET change alters the measured load). Victim and interferer tasks are both included because the mapping can move any task. The application-cluster DMA engine is an unnamed bus master that can contend for the SRAM port, so dma is included. report.INT is the record itself. Excluded artifacts: MPU partition entries and index (they affect spatial isolation, not port timing), CAN/E2E/security artifacts, the item definition, and the HIL rig (the measurement was on target, not on the HIL rig). INT is a direct measurement and consumes no other evidence result. RTA results consume INT, not the reverse.

answer.rationale: RTA:A3 is the response-time analysis for core A3. It depends directly on four inputs. First, A3's allocation row (alloc.A3), which sets the task set A3t0, A3t1 and A3t2. Second, each of those tasks' timing parameters (WCET and period), which drive the response-time recurrence. Third, each task's memory-access parameters (SRAM use and access rate), which scale the per-access interference delay. Fourth, the interference report file (report.INT), the result of evidence INT, which supplies the per-access shared-SRAM-port interference bound. Interference from co-runners on the shared SRAM port (I0, I1, A0-A2 allocations and their tasks' mem parameters, plus the ic arbitration configuration) affects this result only through INT, which RTA:A3 consumes. Those artifacts are therefore covered transitively via INT and are not repeated here; the reviewer should confirm INT's own scope includes them. WCET values enter through the tim.* artifacts, so the static-analysis (SA:A3t*) results are not consumed directly. Excluded because RTA:A3 cannot depend on them: code units, MPU partition entries and index, DMA, CAN and E2E items, security architecture, HIL rig, item definition, built images, the other cores' RTAs, and the UT, HARA and TARA evidence.

answer.rationale: INT is an on-target measurement of shared-SRAM port interference. The report states it is valid only for the current task-to-core mapping and the current arbitration settings. That makes every allocation row and the interconnect config (arbitration, slot latency, which clusters are wired to the port) part of the scope. All six cores reach the port, so the result also depends on every task's memory-access parameters (SRAM use, access rate). It depends on every task's timing parameters too, because periods and WCETs set how dense the access traffic is. The application-cluster DMA engine is another bus master that can contend for the port, so dma is included even though the report does not name it. The measurement ran the built images. Both images and all task source units are therefore included, since any code change alters the measured access behaviour. report.INT itself is included. Excluded as unable to affect contention timing: MPU partition entries and index, CAN, E2E library, security architecture, HIL rig and item definition. The rig is excluded because the measurement was on target, not on the HIL rig. INT is a direct measurement and consumes no other evidence result. RTA and WCET evidence more likely consume INT than the reverse.

answer.rationale: The MPU-Check verifies that the MPU partition entries listed in the partition table do not overlap. Its result depends on the content of each checked entry (all 12 part.* entries for the island tasks BrakeCtl, I0t0-I0t3, I1t0-I1t5 and WSpeed). It also depends on part.index, which defines which entries are in the table. A change to the index, such as adding or removing an entry, could change the result. No partition entries exist in the catalogue for application-core tasks, so nothing on the application side is in scope. Several artifacts are excluded because the check compares only partition entries: timing, memory-access and code parameters, allocation rows, interconnect, DMA, and built images. Changes to the address ranges a task actually needs are a separate concern for static analysis or coverage checks. The report does not consume the result of any other evidence item. Whether DMA or application-cluster masters can bypass MPU protection belongs to a separate freedom-from-interference argument, not this overlap check; a reviewer may want to confirm that boundary.

It also depends on the table index, because the index decides which entries exist; adding or removing an entry could introduce an overlap. Application-cluster tasks have no part.* entries in the catalogue, so they are not part of this table. The check does not depend on timing, memory-access rates, source code, allocation rows, interconnect, DMA or built images. Those could matter if the MPU configuration were derived from the built image or from linker output, but the report checks the partition table entries directly. The report shows no consumption of other evidence results. One point for the reviewer: the report lists the entries it checked rather than deriving them. If part.index changes, it should be re-checked to confirm the checked set still matches the indexed set.

The multicore interference bounds are imported from the INT result (file report.INT). Those bounds depend on: which tasks the other cores sharing the island SRAM port run (alloc.A0, A1, A3, I0, I1); those tasks' memory-access parameters (all non-A2 mem.* entries, since each task's core is fixed by the alloc rows); port arbitration, slot latency and wiring (ic); and application-cluster DMA traffic on the port (dma). Timing parameters of tasks on other cores are excluded on the assumption that interference is bounded from access rates. answer.rationale:
INT measures the worst per-access delay seen by the island cores at the shared island SRAM port. The result therefore depends on:
- the report file itself;
- the measured images (img.island, img.app) and the measurement setup (rig);
- the port arbitration and slot latency, and which clusters are wired to the port (ic);
- every source of contending traffic on that port: the allocation rows of all six cores and the SRAM-use and access-rate parameters of every task. BrakeCtl and WSpeed are included because the catalogue does not say which core they run on.
- application-cluster DMA (dma), which can also reach the port.

The report names only img.app explicitly, but A0-A3 share the port, so application co-runners are an implicit dependency. Flag for the reviewer: the log says co-runner load was generated only on I0 and I1. Application-cluster contention may therefore not be covered, and the result may not bound interference from A0-A3 or from DMA.

Excluded:
- Code units are excluded because their effect on the measurement reaches it through the built images and the memory parameters.
- tim.* is excluded because access rates are captured in mem.*. The reviewer may add it if access rate is derived from period.
- MPU partitions, CAN, E2E, security and item artifacts are excluded because they do not affect port timing.

INT is a direct measurement and consumes no other evidence result.

answer.rationale: INT is an on-target measurement of shared-SRAM port interference under the normal load of all cores plus stress kernels. The report names two dependencies: the task-to-core mapping (all six alloc rows) and the interconnect arbitration settings (ic). ic also covers slot latency and which clusters are wired to the port. The measured contention also depends on several things the report does not name. First, every task's SRAM access behaviour (mem.*). Second, how often each task runs (tim.*, since the period sets the access rate). Third, the actual code executing on each core (code.* for every task, plus the e2e library linked into them), as realised in the built images img.island and img.app. Application-cluster DMA traffic (dma) can also contend for the port. All cores are included because, without the ic wiring details, either cluster may reach the port. The report file itself is in scope. Excluded: MPU partition entries and index (they do not affect port timing); CAN matrix, security architecture, item definition and HIL rig (the measurement was on target, not on the rig). INT is a direct measurement and does not consume results from SA, RTA, UT or other evidence; those analyses instead consume INT.

All six cores ran contenders, so the result depends on: the allocation rows of I0, I1 and A0-A3, which decide what runs where; the SRAM-use and access-rate parameters of every task that can reach the port, including BrakeCtl and WSpeed, whose core is not stated; the interconnect configuration (arbitration, the 50 ns slot setting, which clusters are wired to the port); and the application-cluster DMA engine, which also contends for the port. It also depends on the HIL-B2 rig configuration, the two built images under test (island-fw-build-531, app-fw-build-140) and the report file itself. Task code is not listed separately because a code change takes effect through the images already in scope. WCET/period parameters, MPU partitions, CAN, security and E2E artifacts are excluded: they do not determine the measured port contention. That leaves one judgement call for the reviewer: task periods (tim.*) are not deterministically irrelevant, since a period change would alter contender access patterns, so whether to add them is left to the engineer. INT is a primary measurement; it does not take any other evidence item's result as input, though RTA results likely consume it.

Response-time analysis of core I1 takes the I1t1 period directly as input, and the 100 ms to 2 ms change sharply raises I1t1's utilisation and preemption of lower-priority I1 tasks (including WSpeed); it also consumes the refreshed INT results.
Core I0's response times (including BrakeCtl) use interference bounds from INT, which change because I1t1 now accesses the shared island SRAM port far more often.
Core A0's response-time analysis consumes the INT interference bounds, which are stale because I1t1's SRAM access frequency rose 50x.
Core A1's response-time analysis consumes the INT interference bounds, which are stale because I1t1's SRAM access frequency rose 50x.
Core A2's response-time analysis consumes the INT interference bounds, which are stale because I1t1's SRAM access frequency rose 50x.
Core A3's response-time analysis consumes the INT interference bounds, which are stale because I1t1's SRAM access frequency rose 50x.

The HIL tests run the rebuilt img.island with the new 2 ms I1t1 schedule, so system-level timing and behaviour on the rig must be re-demonstrated; this is independent but expensive, so it is scheduled last.

extra.reason: If code.I1t1 embeds its sample time (e.g. a dt constant in filters, integrators or debounce counters) that was not updated with the 100 ms to 2 ms period change, functional behaviour changes even though the code hash did not, and unit tests built on the old timing assumption no longer show correct behaviour at the new rate; no scope links code-level tests to tim.I1t1.

Static analysis of I1t1 may carry period-dependent assumptions such as the WCET bound, numeric ranges of time-scaled quantities, or overflow of tick counters; these could be invalidated by a 50x faster activation even though code.I1t1 is unchanged.

If I1t1 sends or receives CAN messages, their cycle time changes with the task period while the can matrix (cycle times, E2E counter or timeout parameters) was not updated, so E2E timeout and alive-counter evidence may be stale; this dependency of the can matrix on task periods is not recorded in any scope.

answer.rationale: The E2E Profile 5 conformance result is a check of the configured E2E protection (Data ID, length, counter and CRC settings) of the listed messages, held in the CAN communication matrix ('can'). It runs against the E2E_P05 library implementation ('code.e2e', v2.1). Changing the protected messages or their parameters, or the library, could change the verdict. It is a static protocol and configuration conformance check, not a timing or interference result. So allocation rows, task timing and memory parameters, MPU entries, interconnect, DMA and the other evidence items do not feed it. Points for the reviewer: (1) If the check was run against the integrated build rather than the library and matrix alone, img.island and/or img.app should be added. (2) If BrakeReq is produced or consumed by a specific task's code that calls the library (e.g. BrakeCtl), the reviewer may consider adding that task's code unit (e.g. code.BrakeCtl). The report gives no basis for either addition.

The A1 schedulability result also depends on the interference delay A1 suffers at the shared island SRAM port. That delay depends on the following: (1) the interconnect configuration (ic): arbitration, slot latency, and which clusters are wired to the port. (2) The application DMA engine (dma), which also issues port traffic. (3) Which tasks run on the other cores (alloc.A0, A2, A3, I0, I1). (4) Those tasks' memory-access parameters (mem.*) and periods/WCETs (tim.*), which bound their access counts per window. BrakeCtl and WSpeed are included because they are island-resident tasks that can reach the port. Their allocation is presumably captured in alloc.I0/I1, but a reviewer should confirm this. Excluded items and why: (a) Source code and built images affect the result only through the tim/mem parameters. (b) MPU partition entries, CAN, E2E, security, rig and item artifacts do not enter response-time analysis. (c) SA/UT evidence is not consumed directly, since the WCETs come from the tim.* parameters.

answer.rationale: RTA:A3 analyses the tasks mapped to A3 by alloc.A3 (A3t0-A3t2), using their timing and memory parameters (tim/mem.A3t*). It reads the inflated execution times from the interference analysis, so it consumes INT, and the report file report.INT is in scope. Those inflated times depend on contention at the shared island SRAM port. That contention is set by: the arbitration and slot latency in ic; what runs on every other core reaching the port (alloc.I0, I1, A0, A1, A2); and the SRAM access parameters (mem.*) of all those tasks. BrakeCtl and WSpeed are included because their core assignment is not stated in the catalogue. These are included as transitive dependencies through INT. Excluded: code units, MPU partitions, CAN/E2E, security, HIL, item, images, and SA/UT evidence, because the report says WCETs come from the task configuration, not from static analysis. Also excluded: tim.* of other-core tasks, since contention is taken to be captured by their mem access rates. Reviewer checks: (1) whether the dma engine generates SRAM-port traffic, in which case dma should be added; (2) whether INT uses other-core periods, in which case those tim.* entries should be added.

answer.rationale: The MPU-Check is a static non-overlap check over the MPU partition table. Its result can change only if one of the checked entries changes or if the table index changes. A changed index could add, remove or substitute an entry and so create an overlap that is not in the current entry list. That is why part.index belongs in scope along with all ten part.* entries. The check reads only partition address and region data. It does not read timing, memory-access rate, source code, interconnect, DMA, the built images, or results from other evidence, so it consumes no other evidence item. The allocation rows (alloc.I0 and alloc.I1) are left out because the check as reported compares entries listed in the index regardless of core placement. The reviewer should confirm this. If the tool checks overlap per core or per MPU instance, alloc.I0 and alloc.I1 should be added.

answer.rationale: Response-time analysis of core A0 depends on four things. First, A0's task set (alloc.A0). Second, each A0 task's WCET and period (tim.A0t*) and SRAM access parameters (mem.A0t*). Third, the interference bound in report.INT, taken from evidence INT. Fourth, the per-task WCETs, which come from the static WCET analyses SA:A0t0-SA:A0t5. Code changes reach this result only through those SA results, so code.A0t* is not in scope directly. Multicore interference on the shared island SRAM port depends on factors the report does not name: port arbitration and slot latency (ic), application-cluster DMA traffic (dma), and the co-runners on A1-A3 (alloc.A1-A3 and their mem.* access parameters). These are listed so the result is rechecked directly if any of them change. Under the current interconnect only the application cluster is wired to the port, so island-core tasks, MPU, CAN/E2E, security, HIL and image artifacts are excluded. A change to ic that wires the island to the port would itself trigger review. The reviewer should confirm two assumptions. One is that the interference model uses per-task access rates rather than other-core WCETs and periods; if it does not, tim.A1-A3 should be added. The other is that the island cluster is not wired to the port.

answer.rationale: This is the response-time analysis for core I0 (SafetyCore0). It depends on I0's allocation row, which sets the task set: BrakeCtl (Brake_Control_5ms) plus I0t0-I0t4 (SafetyCore0_Runnable0-4). It uses each task's timing parameters (WCET, period) and memory-access parameters (the access rate scales SRAM-port interference). The WCET values come from the per-task static analyses SA:BrakeCtl and SA:I0t0-I0t4, so the analysis consumes those. It imports multicore interference bounds from interference_bounds.xml, so it consumes the INT evidence and depends on the report.INT file. I did not list the interference inputs (ic arbitration and slot latency, other cores' allocation rows and memory parameters, dma) directly. They reach this result only through INT and would propagate through that consumed dependency. If the RTA tool reads ic slot latency directly rather than taking it from the imported bounds, the reviewer should add ic to the scope. Excluded as unable to affect this result: code units (used only through SA), MPU partitions, CAN/E2E, security, HIL rig, item definition, and built images.
